---
title: Tamper-Evident Logs
llms-description: Storing a copy of each sample's events in an add-only S3 bucket while an eval runs, then checking .eval files against it with inspect validate.
---

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
Tamper-evident logs are experimental. The option, the store layout and the output of `inspect validate` are not yet a stable API and can change without notice.
:::

## Overview

An eval log (a `.eval` file) can be changed after it is written, either by someone with write access to the log directory or by the eval process itself if it is compromised while it runs. Tamper-evident logs let you detect such changes.

While an eval runs, each sample writes its events to an *add-only store*: an S3 bucket in a separate AWS account, where the eval host can add objects but cannot change or delete them. A sample writes to the store at the following points:

-   Before each model call sends its request.
-   Before each set of tool calls starts.
-   At the end of the sample, after scoring.

At each of these points the sample waits until S3 confirms the write. Later, you can use the `inspect validate` command to compare the `.eval` files with the add-only store and report each difference.

Below we'll cover what tamper-evident logs do and don't protect, how to set up the add-only store, and how to run evals and validate their logs.

## What Is Protected

Tamper-evident logs protect against the following:

-   **Edits to a finished log.** If someone changes a sample's events or scores, deletes or adds a sample, or replaces the `.eval` file, `inspect validate` will report it. The original events remain in the add-only store.

-   **Edits by a compromised eval process.** Events that the store confirmed before the compromise can't be changed. If the process changes them in its local copy, the `.eval` file will no longer match the store.

-   **Lost samples.** Each sample attempt writes a closing record at its end. If a sample has a closing record but isn't in the `.eval` file, the validator reports `missing_sample`. The exception is an eval that stopped before it finished its `.eval` file (see [What Is Not Protected](#what-is-not-protected) below).

## What Is Not Protected

There are also a number of things that tamper-evident logs do not protect against:

-   **Anything the process writes after it is compromised.** A compromised process can write false events to the store, using the correct secret for its eval. Events that the sample recorded after its last confirmed write (but before the compromise) are also not protected.

-   **A whole fake eval.** A compromised eval host can write the records of an eval that never ran. The validator reports it only if no `.eval` file has its eval id.

-   **An attempt or eval that stops writing.** A compromised process can stop writing before a closing record. The validator lists the attempt or eval as `stopped`, but does not compare a stopped attempt's events (or a stopped eval's status, stats and results) with the `.eval` file.

-   **A sample that a retry stopped running.** A retry's `.eval` file can keep the earlier eval's copy of a sample that the retry stopped writing. The validator compares that copy with the records of the nearest earlier eval that closed the sample, so the retry's own stored events for the sample are not compared (its attempt is listed as `stopped`).

-   **Samples deleted from the `.eval` file of an eval that stopped.** If an eval stopped before it finished its `.eval` file, a sample deleted from that file shows up as a `not_logged` line rather than a finding.

-   **A deleted `.eval` file of an eval that a later eval names.** This shows up as a `prior_without_file` line rather than a finding. Note that eval-host keys can forge such a later eval.

-   **Fields that are not stored.** The validator checks each sample's events and scores, which samples the `.eval` file has, and the eval's status, stats and results. It does not check other fields (for example the eval spec and plan, each sample's messages, output and error, or the sample summaries).

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
A pass shows that the `.eval` file matches what was stored. It does not show that the run was honest.
:::

See [Validation edge cases](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai/blob/main/design/tamper-evident-logs-findings.md#validation-edge-cases) in the design notes for the details of these cases.

## Store Setup

To set up the add-only store you'll use two AWS accounts:

-   The bucket's account, which holds the bucket and the validator's role.
-   The eval hosts' account, which holds the eval hosts and their role.

People who can sign in to an eval host must not be able to change the bucket's settings. AWS allows a request from another account only when both the bucket policy and the caller's own IAM policy allow it (see [cross-account policy evaluation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic-cross-account.html)). This means that the eval hosts' role needs an `Allow` in both the bucket policy and its own IAM policy.

Here are the steps required to create the store:

1.  In the bucket's account, create the bucket with Object Lock in COMPLIANCE mode (this also turns on versioning). Set the retention period to the length of time that you must keep the records. Until the period ends, nobody can delete a stored version or make the retention shorter.

    ``` bash
    aws s3api create-bucket --bucket my-addonly-store --region us-east-1 \
      --object-lock-enabled-for-bucket
    aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket my-addonly-store \
      --object-lock-configuration '{"ObjectLockEnabled": "Enabled",
        "Rule": {"DefaultRetention": {"Mode": "COMPLIANCE", "Days": 365}}}'
    ```

    For a region other than `us-east-1`, you'll also need to pass `--create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=<region>`.

    Keep the default Object Ownership setting (`BucketOwnerEnforced`). With this setting, the bucket's account owns each record that the eval hosts add (see [Object Ownership](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/about-object-ownership.html)).

2.  In the eval hosts' account, create the `eval-host` role with an IAM policy that can only add objects and read the Object Lock settings. The eval gets these credentials using the usual AWS credential chain (for example `AWS_PROFILE` or the instance role).

    ``` json
    {
      "Version": "2012-10-17",
      "Statement": [
        {
          "Effect": "Allow",
          "Action": "s3:PutObject",
          "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-addonly-store/*"
        },
        {
          "Effect": "Allow",
          "Action": "s3:GetBucketObjectLockConfiguration",
          "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-addonly-store"
        }
      ]
    }
    ```

3.  Add a bucket policy. Its first statement refuses a put without `If-None-Match` (without this statement, a put can add a second version of an object). The other two statements let the eval hosts' role add objects and read the Object Lock settings. Replace `111122223333` with the ID of the eval hosts' account, and `eval-host` with the name of their role.

    ``` json
    {
      "Version": "2012-10-17",
      "Statement": [
        {
          "Sid": "RequireIfNoneMatch",
          "Effect": "Deny",
          "Principal": "*",
          "Action": "s3:PutObject",
          "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-addonly-store/*",
          "Condition": {"Null": {"s3:if-none-match": "true"}}
        },
        {
          "Sid": "EvalHostPut",
          "Effect": "Allow",
          "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/eval-host"},
          "Action": "s3:PutObject",
          "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-addonly-store/*"
        },
        {
          "Sid": "EvalHostReadObjectLock",
          "Effect": "Allow",
          "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/eval-host"},
          "Action": "s3:GetBucketObjectLockConfiguration",
          "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-addonly-store"
        }
      ]
    }
    ```

    Don't allow the eval hosts' role anything else. The [start check](#start-check) fails if the role can read or delete a record.

4.  In the bucket's account, create a read-only role for the validator. The validator reads the bucket policy, and S3 refuses that read to every other account (see [GetBucketPolicy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/API/API_GetBucketPolicy.html)), so a validator in another account cannot check the bucket's settings. Within the bucket's account, the role's own IAM policy is enough:

    ``` json
    {
      "Version": "2012-10-17",
      "Statement": [
        {
          "Effect": "Allow",
          "Action": [
            "s3:ListBucketVersions",
            "s3:GetBucketVersioning",
            "s3:GetBucketPolicy",
            "s3:GetBucketObjectLockConfiguration"
          ],
          "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-addonly-store"
        },
        {
          "Effect": "Allow",
          "Action": "s3:GetObjectVersion",
          "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-addonly-store/*"
        }
      ]
    }
    ```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Use one prefix in the bucket for each log directory. The validator reports every eval under its prefix that has no `.eval` file in the log directory, so evals from other log directories must not share the prefix.
:::

## Running Evals

To enable tamper-evident logs, pass the location of the add-only store when you run an eval. For example:

``` bash
inspect eval ctf.py --model openai/gpt-6-luna \
  --tamper-evident-store s3://my-addonly-store/team-a
```

Or from Python:

``` python
eval("ctf.py", model="openai/gpt-6-luna",
     tamper_evident_store="s3://my-addonly-store/team-a")
```

The `eval_set()` function and `inspect eval-set` command take the same option, and use it for each retry that they run. If you don't provide the option, the eval writes nothing to the add-only store.

### Start Check

Before the first sample starts, the eval runs a series of checks against the store:

1.  It writes its first record.
2.  It writes the record again (S3 must refuse).
3.  It tries to read and delete the record (S3 must refuse).
4.  It reads the Object Lock settings (they must be COMPLIANCE).

If any check fails, the eval fails.

The eval also requires `log_realtime` (which is on by default), and will fail at start if `log_realtime` is off.

### Errors and Cancellation

If a write fails with a network error, throttling or a server error, the sample will retry it for up to 60 seconds. If the write still fails (or fails for another reason), the eval fails regardless of what `fail_on_error` says. This includes a write that S3 refuses because the object already exists.

When an eval is cancelled or stops on an error, each sample that has already been scored still writes its closing record and is logged. A sample that is cancelled or reaches its time limit during a write will finish that write first. Note that if S3 fails, the eval waits while each of these writes retries for up to 60 seconds.

### Retries

The log does not record the store location, so you'll need to provide it again when you retry an eval with `eval_retry()` or `inspect eval-retry`. For example:

``` bash
inspect eval-retry logs/2026-11-22T10-00-00_ctf_abc.eval \
  --tamper-evident-store s3://my-addonly-store/team-a
```

`eval_set()` and `task_retry_attempts` retry a failed eval within the same run, and use the store location that the run was given. However, when you run `eval_set()` again to retry the evals of an earlier run, you need to provide the store location again.

A sample that a retry reuses from the earlier eval is not written again. Rather, the retry's start record names the earlier eval, and the validator compares the sample with the records of the eval that ran it (the earlier eval, or an eval before it when the earlier eval was also a retry).

When using `retry_on_error`, the failed attempt keeps its records in the store and has no closing record. The validator lists it as `stopped` and does not report it as a finding.

By default, `eval_set()` deletes the `.eval` file of a failed attempt after its retry (the `retry_cleanup` option). The validator lists the failed attempt's eval as `prior_without_file` rather than as a finding. It still uses that eval's records to check the samples that the retry reused.

## Validating Logs

Use the `inspect validate` command to check a log directory against the add-only store. Run it with the read-only credentials of the validator, and always take the store location from your own configuration, never from a `.eval` file. For example:

``` bash
inspect validate logs --store s3://my-addonly-store/team-a
```

You can also set the store location using the `INSPECT_VALIDATE_STORE` environment variable. Be sure to run the validator on a host that the eval hosts cannot control.

### Pass

When validation passes, the command exits with 0 and prints what it checked:

``` default
1 eval(s), 1 sample(s) compared, 0 finding(s).
Checked against the add-only store: each sample's events and scores, which samples the .eval files have, and each eval's status, stats and results.
Not checked: everything else, including the eval spec and plan, each sample's messages, output and error, what the sample summaries say, invalidation and log_updates.
A pass does not show that the run was honest.
```

Lines that start with `stopped`, `not_logged` or `prior_without_file` may appear before the count. These lines are not findings, and they do not change the exit code. For example:

``` default
stopped LdM2ww.../s0.1/1: No closing record: cut short, or its host stopped writing.
```

See the [Output Reference](#output-reference) below for what each line means.

### Failure

When validation fails, the command exits with 1 and prints one line for each finding, consisting of the kind of finding, the eval id or record key, and a message. For example, here a tool result was changed in the `.eval` file:

``` default
event_mismatch ceb6p9.../s0.1/1: Event 8 (tool FWBdtR...) differs in ['result']; the store has 2 version(s) of it.

1 eval(s), 1 sample(s) compared, 1 finding(s).
```

In this next example, someone used the eval host's keys to add a record to the store after the eval. They don't know the eval's secret (the nonce), as it is in the store's records, which the eval host's keys cannot read. Note that the list of record numbers is shortened here:

``` default
nonce VbcjdG.../s0.1/1/16: Nonce differs from the start record's.
record_count VbcjdG.../s0.1/1: Closing record counts 15 records, store has [1, 2, ..., 16].

1 eval(s), 1 sample(s) compared, 2 finding(s).
```

Use the `--verbose` option to list every record in the store along with the time that S3 received it.

To see the original events of a sample, you can read its records from the add-only store. Each sample attempt has the keys `<eval-id>/<sample-id>.<epoch>/<attempt>/<n>` (one record per write) and `<eval-id>/<sample-id>.<epoch>/<attempt>/closing`.

### Output Reference

The following lines are listed in the output but are not findings, and do not change the exit code:

| Line | What it means | What to do |
|------------------------|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `stopped` | The store has no closing record for this eval or sample attempt. A cancel, an error in another sample, a crash or a retry cuts a run short. A compromised host can also stop writing. The validator still checks each record that the eval or attempt wrote. It does not compare a stopped attempt's events, or a stopped eval's status, stats and results, with the `.eval` file. | Make sure that you know why the run stopped. If you do not, treat what the eval or attempt did as not checked. |
| `not_logged` | The sample attempt wrote its closing record, but the sample is not in the `.eval` file. Shown only for an eval with no closing record whose `.eval` file has the status `started`. | If the eval host crashed or was killed, this is expected: Inspect writes samples to the `.eval` file in groups. Otherwise, someone may have deleted the sample from the file. |
| `prior_without_file` | No `.eval` file has this eval id, and a later eval names this eval as its prior eval. `eval_set()` deletes such files after a retry (`retry_cleanup`). | Make sure that you ran the later eval as a retry of this eval. Eval-host keys can forge the later eval, so a deleted `.eval` file can also show this way. |

The following lines are findings. Each finding makes the command exit with 1:

| Finding | What it means | What to do |
|------------------------|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `settings` | The bucket does not have Object Lock in COMPLIANCE mode, versioning is not on, or the bucket policy has no statement that refuses a put without `If-None-Match`. The validator also reports the last one when it cannot read the bucket policy. | Fix the bucket with the steps in [Store Setup](#store-setup), and run the validator in the bucket's account. While a setting was wrong, someone could change or delete records. |
| `overwrite` | A record has more than one version, or a delete marker. The validator uses the earliest version. | Find out who could write or delete in the bucket. |
| `multipart` | A record was uploaded in parts. The eval never does this. The arrival time of such a record is when the upload started. | Treat the record as written by someone other than the eval. |
| `missing_start` | The store has records under this eval id, but no start record. The validator checks nothing else for this eval, and does not compare its `.eval` file. | Treat the records as forged. The eval writes its start record before any other record. |
| `nonce` | A record's nonce differs from the start record's. The eval host's keys cannot read the nonce from the store. | Treat the record as forged. |
| `sequence_gap` | The sample records of an attempt are not numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on. | In an attempt with a closing record, treat the extra record as forged. In a `stopped` attempt, a crash while two writes were in flight can also cause it. |
| `record_count` | The number of sample records differs from the count in the attempt's closing record. | Treat the extra records, or the closing record, as forged. |
| `late_event_version` | A record has a new version of an event that an earlier record stored complete. | An agent that calls [bridged tools](agent-bridge.qmd#bridged-tools) one at a time causes this in an honest run. Otherwise, treat the new version as a change to an event that the store confirmed. |
| `event_without_uuid` | A stored event has no uuid, or its uuid differs from the id of its buffer row. The eval always writes both. | Treat the record as forged. |
| `malformed_record` | A key that the eval never writes, a record that cannot be read or holds the wrong type of record, or sample records whose events cannot be rebuilt. | Treat the record as forged. The validator still checks the eval's other records. If the events cannot be rebuilt, they are not compared with the `.eval` file. |
| `unlisted_attempt` | The store has records of a sample attempt that the eval closing record does not list. | Treat the attempt as written by someone other than the eval. |
| `unstored_eval` | A `.eval` file in the log directory has an eval id with no records under the store prefix. | Make sure that the store prefix is correct and that the eval ran with `tamper_evident_store`. Otherwise, treat the file as not checked. |
| `duplicate_eval_file` | More than one `.eval` file has this eval id. The validator compares only the first, by file name. | Find out where the copies came from. |
| `missing_eval_file` | The store has an eval with an eval closing record or a closed sample attempt, but no `.eval` file in the log directory has its eval id. | Make sure that the log directory and the store prefix match. Otherwise, someone deleted or moved the `.eval` file. |
| `missing_eval_closing` | The `.eval` file is finished (its status is not `started`), but the store has no eval closing record. | An S3 outage at the end of an honest run can cause this. Otherwise, someone changed the file's status. |
| `eval_mismatch` | The `.eval` file's status, stats or results differ from the eval closing record. | `inspect score` and other tools that change a log after the run cause this. Otherwise, someone changed the file. |
| `unstored_sample` | A sample in the `.eval` file has no attempt with a closing record in the store, for this eval or for the earlier evals that a retry reused samples from. | A failed write to the store, or a failed insert into the sample buffer, causes this in an honest run. The sample then has an error in the `.eval` file. Otherwise, someone added the sample. |
| `missing_sample` | A sample with a closing record in the store is not in the `.eval` file. In a retry, it can also be a sample that the earlier eval completed without an error and that the retry selects. | A retry that stopped early can cause this in an honest run. Otherwise, someone deleted the sample. |
| `event_mismatch` | A sample's events differ from the events rebuilt from the store. The message names the first event that differs. | `inspect score`, and a warning logged from a worker thread during the sample, cause this in an honest run. So does a failed write to the store or the sample buffer while a retry runs a sample again that the earlier eval completed with an error (the message says `reused from`): check the eval's errors for a failed write before treating it as a change. Otherwise, someone changed the events. |
| `score_mismatch` | A sample's scores differ from its closing record. | `inspect score` causes this. Otherwise, someone changed the scores. |

## Limitations

Tamper-evident logs currently have the following known limits:

-   **What a `stopped` line means.** Both an honest cancel or crash and a compromised host that stops writing leave a `stopped` line. The validator does not decide which one occurred, and the same applies to `not_logged`.

-   **Honest runs with a missing closing record.** A failed write to the store or to the sample buffer results in `unstored_sample` for a run that was not changed. If a retry is running a sample again that the earlier eval completed with an error, the result is an `event_mismatch` instead, because the validator compares the retry's copy with the earlier eval's records. Similarly, a failed write of the eval closing record (after the `.eval` file is finished) results in `missing_eval_closing`.

-   **Rescoring.** `inspect score` changes the scores and results, and also writes the sample's events again in a different order. The validator will then report `score_mismatch`, `eval_mismatch` and `event_mismatch`. How to show a rescore separately from tampering is an open question.

-   **Other changes after the run.** A tool that changes the eval's status, stats or results after the run will cause validation to fail, just as a hand edit does. Merged shard logs and samples removed during the run are not yet handled.

-   **A retry that stops early.** In some cases, a retry that stops before it runs a sample results in `missing_sample` for a run that was not changed. A later retry that completes keeps the sample.

-   **A deleted sample that failed in the earlier eval.** A retry also copies the samples that the earlier eval completed with an error. If the retry stops before it runs such a sample again, and someone then deletes the copy from the retry's `.eval` file, the validator will not report it.

-   **Checkpoint resume.** The validator does not check a resumed sample's restored state against the earlier eval's records.

-   **Validation cost.** The validator reads every record of every eval under the prefix, using one S3 request for each record.

-   **Events that skip the sample buffer.** A warning logged from a worker thread during a sample can cause an event to skip the local sample buffer, in which case it never reaches the store. The validator will then report an `event_mismatch` for a run that was not changed.
